props.title: City of Industry
props.initialSlug: Crime boss hunts brother's killers in L.A. heist war

sections.content: City of Industry sits at the intersection of 90s neo-noir and heist films, following the brutal path of revenge taken by Roy Egan (Harvey Keitel) after a jewelry store robbery goes wrong. The film shares DNA with Michael Mann's Heat (1995) in its Los Angeles criminal underworld setting, though it trades Mann's operatic scope for grittier, street-level violence. Director John Irvin brings the same hard-edged sensibility he showed in Raw Deal (1986), creating a throwback to 70s crime films like The Killing of a Chinese Bookie (1976).

sections.content: The film's exploration of loyalty and betrayal among thieves follows a rich tradition in 90s crime cinema, from Reservoir Dogs (1992) to The Usual Suspects (1995). Stephen Dorff's unhinged performance as the treacherous Skip Kovich provides a memorable antagonist, while Keitel delivers the kind of intense, haunted portrayal that defined his work in films like Bad Lieutenant (1992) and Reservoir Dogs. The Los Angeles industrial sprawl becomes a character itself, photographed with a stark brutality that eschews the usual glamorous depictions of the city.

Timothy Hutton and Lucy Liu appear in early supporting roles, with Liu making her feature film debut. The heist sequence shows clear influence from classics like The Asphalt Jungle (1950) and The Killing (1956), demonstrating how the film straddles both classic noir and contemporary crime thriller elements. Director Irvin brings his documentary background to bear in the film's unflinching violence and location shooting. SUBHEAD: Neo-Noir Revival Context

sections.content: City of Industry arrived during a fertile period for neo-noir, alongside films like L.A. Confidential (1997), Lost Highway (1997), and U-Turn (1997). These films updated noir traditions for modern audiences while maintaining core themes of corruption, betrayal, and moral ambiguity. The industrial wastelands and criminal underground of Los Angeles provided perfect settings for these dark narratives, with City of Industry particularly focused on the unglamorous edges of the metropolis.
